title: How do languages connect people?
essentialQuestion: How does language build belonging and understanding?
learningGoal: Explain how languages and other ways of communicating connect people, and why speaking more than one language is a strength.

warmUp.question: How can people share a message if they do not speak the same language?

evidence.label: Fictional example created for this lesson.
evidence.question: Which parts of the notice could someone understand without reading English?

cases.name: Written notice
cases.body: “Free food for everyone: Friday, 4 p.m., Hillside Learning Centre.”

cases.name: Volunteer says
cases.body: “Some visitors read English easily. Others ask a friend to help, look at the pictures, use sign language, or speak another language with one of us.”

cards.title: Picture version of the notice (pictogram)
items: A small map with a pin on the centre

sections.heading: Language helps people connect
sections.text: People use language to share news, jokes, memories and care. Hearing a word you know can help you feel welcome in a new place. Many people in the world are multilingual. In Paraguay, for example, many people speak both Spanish and Guaraní. Someone who speaks Somali, Arabic and English, or Tamil and Malay, can help different groups understand each other. That is a real skill. How well a person speaks English does not show how clever they are. It does not show whether their ideas matter.
sections.simpler: People use language to share news, jokes and care. A word you know can help you feel welcome. Many people are multilingual. They speak two or more languages. In Paraguay, lots of people speak Spanish and Guaraní. If you speak two or three languages, you can help others. That is a real skill. Good English does not show how smart you are. All people's ideas matter.

sections.heading: People communicate in many ways
sections.text: Communication is not only speaking and writing. Deaf communities use sign languages, which are full languages with their own grammar. The United Nations says there are more than 300 sign languages in the world. People also use gestures, pictures and clear design. The pictogram on the notice shows food, a clock, a calendar and a map. This makes the notice more accessible, because more people can understand the main message. But a picture cannot give every detail, such as what to bring. A volunteer who can interpret still helps.
sections.simpler: Communication is more than talking and writing. Deaf people use sign languages. These are full languages. There are more than 300 of them. People also use hands, faces and pictures. The notice has pictures of food, a clock and a map. This makes it more accessible. More people can understand it. But a picture cannot say what to bring. A helper who can interpret is still useful.

sections.heading: Languages change and share words
sections.text: Languages change over time. They also borrow words from each other when people meet and trade. The English word “coffee” travelled a long way. It started as the Arabic word qahwah. It became kahveh in Turkish and caffè in Italian, and then it reached English. Many languages are also related. English, Hindi and Persian belong to one language family, because they grew from one very old language. Arabic, Somali and Hausa belong to another family. No language is better than another. Each one carries the knowledge and stories of the people who speak it.
sections.simpler: Languages change over time. They take words from each other. Look at the word “coffee”. It began in Arabic. Then it went into Turkish and Italian. Then it came into English. Some languages are like cousins. They grew from one old language. So they are in one language family. English, Hindi and Persian are in one. Arabic, Somali and Hausa are in a different one. No language is the best. Each one holds the stories of the people who speak it.

glossary.definition: Able to speak and understand more than one language.
glossary.example: A person who speaks Tamil and Malay is multilingual.

glossary.definition: Sharing ideas or information with other people.
glossary.example: The notice and the pictogram are both kinds of communication.

glossary.definition: Made so that more people can use or understand it.
glossary.example: The pictures make the notice more accessible.

glossary.definition: To help people understand each other across languages.
glossary.example: A volunteer can interpret for a visitor at the centre.

glossary.definition: A group of languages that grew from one older language.
glossary.example: English and Persian belong to the same language family.

checks.question: What is one limit of the pictogram?

options.text: It cannot show every detail, like what to bring.
options.feedback: Yes. The pictures show the main message, but not every detail. A volunteer can help with the rest.

options.text: It means the volunteers never need to talk at all.
options.feedback: Not quite. The lesson says a volunteer who can interpret still helps. Look for what the pictures cannot show.

options.text: It proves that everyone can read English well.
options.feedback: Not quite. The pictures help people who do not read English. Look for what the pictures cannot show.

checks.question: Which idea about languages comes from the lesson?

options.text: Speaking English well shows a person is clever.
options.feedback: Not quite. The lesson says how well someone speaks English does not show how clever they are.

options.text: Only spoken languages are real languages.
options.feedback: Not quite. Sign languages are full languages with their own grammar.

options.text: Languages borrow words, like “coffee” from Arabic.
options.feedback: Yes. “Coffee” came from Arabic, through Turkish and Italian, into English.

checks.question: What else could the centre add so that more people understand the notice?
checks.placeholder: Think about people who cannot read, people who are Deaf, and people who speak other languages ...

write.prompt: Suggest two ways to make the centre's notice clear to more people. Say how each one helps and one thing it cannot do.
selfCheck: I suggested two changes to the notice.
I explained how each change helps.
write.example: I would add the notice in two or three languages that visitors use. This helps because more people can read it in a language they know. I would also add a helper at the door who can interpret. This helps people ask questions, like what to bring. One limit is that a written notice cannot help people who do not read. The pictures and the helper can help with that. This shows that using more than one way to share a message helps more people feel welcome.

speak.partnerTask: Explain the notice to your partner using simple words and a gesture or a drawing. Your partner says what was clear.
speak.independentTask: Explain why speaking more than one language is a useful skill. Use one example from the lesson.

watch.title: How languages evolve
watch.why: This animated TED-Ed lesson shows how languages change over time and why some languages are related.
watch.beforeQuestion: How can two languages be related, like members of a family?
watch.afterQuestion: What does a shared language family tell us, and what does it not tell us?
watch.summary: This animated video explains how languages change. Long ago, groups of people who spoke one language moved apart. They lived in new places and met new neighbours. Over many years, each group changed the way it spoke. New words came in, and sounds changed. In time, one language became several languages. Languages that grew from one older language form a language family. Language experts compare grammar and basic words, like numbers, to find these links. Some words are borrowed from neighbours, so experts check them with care. It can be hard to say where one language ends and another begins. So different experts count between 3,000 and 8,000 languages in the world. The video ends with an idea: a language that sounds new to you may be related to one you know.
keyPoints: Related languages grew from one older language.
Languages also borrow words from their neighbours.
watch.contentNote: The video opens with the Tower of Babel story as a hook, then describes early human groups moving apart. The narration is fast and the vocabulary is quite advanced, so pause often or use the written summary.

educatorNotes: Many learners speak two or three languages. Celebrate this, but do not ask learners to name their home languages or to speak them in front of others. Let anyone who wants to share do so.
Accents and levels of English differ a lot in any group. Model patience, and never correct pronunciation in a way that embarrasses someone.
You could add a local example of a borrowed word (for instance, a word the local language shares with Arabic, English or Dutch), or show the centre notice in the languages your learners use.
changes: Expanded the reading from about 110 to about 280 words, adding sign languages, borrowed words (how “coffee” travelled from Arabic into English) and language families.
Added a clear message that speaking more than one language is a strength, with examples from South America, Africa, the Middle East and Asia.
Removed the Base44 line addressed to teachers from the learner text and moved that guidance into educatorNotes.
Lightly reworded the fictional notice from “Food distribution” to “Free food for everyone” and named the centre (Hillside) so it is easier to read.
